title: Complexity of Clathrin Coat Dynamics in Endocytosis

sections.title: 研究问题
sections.text:
《Complexity of Clathrin Coat Dynamics in Endocytosis》：研究问题的原文依据。

【Introduction · tra70052-sec-0002-p1】Clathrin‐mediated endocytosis is a major pathway eukaryotic cells use for the selective uptake of a wide range of molecules, from hormones and transmembrane proteins to lipids and nutrients. It is a highly conserved internalisation route found across the eukaryotic phylogenetic tree, making it one of the most studied trafficking pathways across model organisms from mammals to plants and fungi, which has provided a good understanding of the inner workings of this complex process.

【Introduction · tra70052-sec-0002-p2】Clathrin‐mediated endocytosis involves the controlled deformation of the plasma membrane into a cargo‐filled vesicle and is characterised by the sequential and tightly regulated assembly of over 50 proteins into a complex structure. These proteins coordinate their activities to (1) initiate the endocytic process at specific locations on the plasma membrane; (2) select and capture molecules to be internalised; (3) deform the plasma membrane in an inward orientation; and (4) cut the newly formed clathrin‐coated vesicle from the plasma membrane, without compromising its integrity (Figure 1). After scission, the endocytic vesicles are rapidly uncoated and are subsequently transported to fuse with endosomes. In 1964, Roth and Porter [1], who used electron microscopy imaging to track the internalisation of electron‐dense yolk granules in mosquito oocytes, described for the first time the characteristic “bristle coats” decorating the endocytic pits and vesicles. The main component of the bristle coats, clathrin, was later identified by Barbara Pearse [2]. Subsequent work, in parallel with progress in imaging techniques, has gradually completed the picture first drawn by these founding studies, progressively identifying and characterising the many pieces of the endocytic puzzle, from adaptor proteins to the myriad of effectors and regulatory proteins, as well as the specific lipid species required for coat formation. Although the structural properties and sequential recruitment of the key players of the endocytic machinery have been described in great detail over the years, our understanding of the many parameters controlling their assembly remains poor. This is also true for clathrin, despite it being arguably one of the best characterised proteins of membrane traffic in general. While clathrin's assembly at endocytic sites is well understood from a structural standpoint, how this assembly is controlled dynamically as the endocytic vesicle is formed is still unclear. Although it was long thought to have a structural support function for the forming vesicle, a growing body of evidence is highlighting a more dynamic role for clathrin in regulating the progression of the endocytic event. In this review, we focus on the dynamic properties of clathrin assembly at endocytic sites and discuss how these properties may govern endocytic progression. We summarise experimental data pointing at potential roles of clathrin exchange in membrane deformation, cargo recruitment as well as endocytic site architectural organisation, and discuss how these various functions might occur concomitantly to ensure successful endocytic vesicle formation.

sections.text:
《Complexity of Clathrin Coat Dynamics in Endocytosis》：结果的原文依据；数值与适用人群以引文为准。

【Introduction · tra70052-sec-0002-p1】Clathrin‐mediated endocytosis is a major pathway eukaryotic cells use for the selective uptake of a wide range of molecules, from hormones and transmembrane proteins to lipids and nutrients. It is a highly conserved internalisation route found across the eukaryotic phylogenetic tree, making it one of the most studied trafficking pathways across model organisms from mammals to plants and fungi, which has provided a good understanding of the inner workings of this complex process.

【Structure of Clathrin and Clathrin Lattices · tra70052-sec-0004-p1】The conservation of clathrin is exemplified by its highly recognisable triskelion shape in many organisms. Clathrin triskelion is a heteromeric complex, composed of three clathrin heavy chains and three clathrin light chains. Clathrin assembles spontaneously into triskelia that constitute the smallest clathrin assemblies that can be found in cells [3, 4, 5].
